title: Astronomer's Notebook: Bits and pieces of Halley's Comet
excerpt: The Orionid Meteor Shower peaks this week. It is the result of the Earth passing through the debris field of Halley’s Comet.
content:
The Orionid Meteor Shower

On the night of Oct. 21-22, meteors will appear to radiate from “the club” of Orion, the Hunter, just below the feet of Gemini.

The meteors will be best viewed after the moon sets, around 3:30 a.m. That gives observers an approximately three-hour window to view meteors

The fragments that produce them being only about the size of sand grains to peas and zipping along at 150,000 miles per hour, or nearly 200 times the speed of sound, as they enter the atmosphere.

Although the meteors appear to emanate from Orion, the shower produces both long- and short-trail meteors that can be viewed in nearly any part of the sky.

Most cometary meteoroids are of low density and fragile, like the carbonaceous pieces of burned leaves or cigarette ashes.

None of these tiny fragments reach the ground. They disintegrate at altitudes of 50 to 60 miles. The Orionids last about a week,  centered on Oct. 21. The peak meteor rate may reach 50 to 70 per hour in some years.

Occasionally, large meteors, called fireballs or bolides, become unusually bright and explode high in the atmosphere. Where do these meteoric particles, called meteoroids, come from?

A trail of comet debris

Twice each year the Earth’s orbit takes it through a swarm of debris trailing from Halley’s Comet.

The first encounter occurs in April, resulting in the Eta Aquarid Meteor Shower, so named because the meteors appear to originate from a point near the star Eta Aquarii in the constellation Aquarius.

The second encounter occurs a half year later in October on the other side of Earth’s orbit, when the meteors appear to be streaking away from the constellation Orion, hence the designation the Orionid Meteor Shower.

Halley’s Comet has an orbital period of about 76 years. Its closest approach to the sun, called perihelion, is 55 million miles and its farthest, aphelion, is 3.3 billion miles.

Each time Halley’s Comet passes through the inner solar system, intense sunlight sublimates some of the surface ice, allowing small rock particles to break away from the comet.

These particles continue the comet’s trajectory and, when Earth passes through cometary debris, burn up in the upper atmosphere, producing the luminous streaks we call meteors.

But when and how did astronomers make the connection between these well-known meteor showers and comets?

The comet-meteor-shower connection

As early as 1861, the American astronomer Daniel Kirkwood (1814-1895) argued that meteors are produced by the litter left behind by comets.

In 1866 the Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli (1835-1910) discovered that the Perseid Meteor Shower occurred whenever Earth crossed the orbit of Comet 1862 III, now known as Swift-Tuttle.

He reasoned that the Perseid particles, small bits of debris ejected from the comet, were spread out along its orbit.

Other prominent meteor showers were found to be associated with known comets, including the Lyrids on April 21 from Comet Thatcher, the Draconids on Oct. 10 from Comet Giacobini-Zinner, the Taurids on Nov. 7, the results of Comet Encke, the Leonids on Nov. 16 from the Comet Tempel-Tuttle debris, and the Geminids on Dec. 12, which are due to 3200 Phaeton, an asteroid.

Edmund Halley’s legacy

Historical analyses revealed that Halley’s Comet has been recorded 30 times, the first of which was in 240 B.C. in Chinese diaries.

In 1696, Edmund Halley (1656-1742), a friend and colleague of Isaac Newton (1642-1727), reported to the Royal Society of London that the comets seen in 1531, 1607 and 1682 had nearly identical orbits, and he therefore concluded that these appearances were due to the same comet returning to the inner solar system every 76 years.

Halley predicted that this comet would return in 1758, and indeed it did. Halley had died years earlier, but his prediction was remembered by astronomers, who named the comet after Halley in honor of his discovery.

A dirty iceberg

The most recent appearance of Halley’s Comet was in 1986, three decades after the start of the space age, when five spacecraft visited the comet.

One of those spacecrafts, the European Space Agency’s Giotto, flew within 370 miles of the nucleus and beamed back to Earth the first ever close-up pictures of a comet nucleus.

The pictures showed a blackish, peanut shaped nucleus 10 miles long emitting jets of gas from its surface. The results confirmed the “dirty iceberg model” of Harvard astronomer Fred Whipple that he first proposed in 1951, in which the comet nucleus is composed of a mixture of volatile — meaning having low boiling points — ices, such as water, carbon dioxide and ammonia, and coated with dust and grit.

The fate of Halley’s Comet

Halley’s Comet reached the farthest orbital point from the sun in December 2023, after which it began its journey back to the inner solar system.

Its next closest approach to Earth will be in July 2061, and after that in May 2134.

Most of the snow that comprises its nucleus is water ice, and Halley’s Comet loses, via sublimation, a surface layer approximately 6 feet deep every time it passes through the inner solar system and is heated by the sun’s rays.

At this rate, Halley’s Comet may survive another 200,000 years, during which time its appearance — and the associated Orionid Meteor Shower — will undoubtedly continue to awe, frighten, and delight the inhabitants of planet Earth, as they have done over past millennia.

Augensen is the director of the Widener University Observatory and emeritus professor of physics and astronomy at Widener University.
